draft.title: Writing ionic formulas
card: An ionic compound has no overall charge. The total positive charge from the cations must equal the total negative charge from the anions.

To write a formula, find the charge on each ion, then choose the numbers of each ion that cancel out. Write the cation first. Magnesium (Mg²⁺) and chloride (Cl⁻) need one Mg²⁺ and two Cl⁻, so the formula is MgCl₂.

A polyatomic ion is a group of atoms with one overall charge, such as sulfate (SO₄²⁻) and nitrate (NO₃⁻). If you need more than one, put the whole ion in brackets and write the number after it, as in Al₂(SO₄)₃ or Ca(NO₃)₂.

To name the compound, write the cation name, then the anion name. A single-atom anion ends in -ide, such as chloride. Polyatomic ions keep their own names, such as sulfate. The numbers in the formula are not part of the name.
draft.remember: Make the positive and negative charges add to zero, and bracket a polyatomic ion when you need more than one.

a.q: Which is the correct formula for calcium nitrate, made from Ca²⁺ and NO₃⁻ ions?
a.why: One Ca²⁺ has a charge of +2, so it needs two NO₃⁻ ions to balance it. The whole nitrate ion goes in brackets before the 2. CaNO₃ is wrong because its charges add to +1, not zero.
a.clue: How many NO₃⁻ ions cancel one 2+ charge?

b.q: Aluminium ions are Al³⁺ and sulfate ions are SO₄²⁻. What is the formula of aluminium sulfate?
b.why: Two Al³⁺ give +6 and three SO₄²⁻ give -6, so the charges cancel. The sulfate is in brackets because more than one is needed. Al₃(SO₄)₂ is a tempting swap of the numbers, but it gives +9 and -4.
b.clue: Find the smallest total charge that both 3 and 2 divide into.

problems.detail: The card gives Ca(NO₃)₂ word for word as its bracket example, so a student can match the answer from the card without balancing any charges.
Ca(NO₃)₂ is the only option with brackets, so a student can pick it from the remember line's 'bracket a polyatomic ion' alone, without working out how many nitrate ions are needed.
The card gives Al₂(SO₄)₃ word for word as an example, so the question tests recall of the card's example rather than the method of balancing charges.

a.q: Potassium ions are K⁺ and sulfate ions are SO₄²⁻. What is the formula of potassium sulfate?
a.why: Two K⁺ give +2, which cancels one SO₄²⁻. Only one sulfate is needed, so it takes no brackets. K(SO₄)₂ swaps the numbers and gives +1 and -4, which do not cancel.
a.clue: How many K⁺ ions cancel one 2- charge?

b.q: Aluminium ions are Al³⁺ and sulfate ions are SO₄²⁻. What is the formula of aluminium sulfate?
b.why: Two Al³⁺ give +6 and three SO₄²⁻ give -6, so the charges cancel. More than one sulfate is needed, so it goes in brackets. Al₃(SO₄)₂ is a tempting swap of the numbers, but it gives +9 and -4.
b.clue: Find the smallest total charge that both 3 and 2 divide into.
